summary: This paper presents an automated bibliometric audit of 1644 metaheuristics papers published in Scientific Reports (2024-2025). Using a mix of regex parsing and LLM-based image reading, it evaluates whether the printed tables (means, standard deviations, run counts) provide sufficient evidence to support the bolding of the 'best' cells. The authors apply a Welch's t-test to the printed summaries and find that in 34.5% of testable cases, the bold cell cannot be statistically separated from the runner-up. The paper highlights a stark difference in reporting quality between papers proposing new optimizers and those applying existing ones.
strengths: The paper addresses a critical reproducibility issue in our community. The methodology is highly transparent, pre-registered, and the distinction between 'new optimizer' and 'application' papers accurately reflects the sociological divide in the field. The authors are also commendably honest about the limitations of their automated parsers.

objections.objection: The paper relies heavily on an LLM (Gemini) to extract data from separate-column and separate-row layouts, which constitute the majority of the testable data. Validating one LLM with another LLM (Claude) is unacceptable for a formal audit of human scientists.
objections.what_would_fix_it: Have a human expert label the 100-item separate-column and Mean/Std-row kits. Report the precision and recall of the LLM reader against this human ground truth, rather than relying on Claude 5's agreement.
objections.quote: no person has yet labelled the released kits.

objections.objection: The paper applies Welch's t-test to CEC benchmark data, which is often bounded at zero and heavily skewed. The community explicitly moved to Wilcoxon/Friedman (García 2009) precisely because t-tests are mathematically invalid for this data. Including cases where the t-test is obviously invalid inflates the headline failure rate.
objections.what_would_fix_it: Do not pool the mathematically invalid t-test cases into the headline 34.5% failure rate. Use the 31.3% figure (where the summaries do not cap a t-statistic) as the primary headline metric in the abstract and conclusion.
objections.quote: The failure rate is 49.0% on the 147 groups with a deviation at least the mean, 47.1% on the 104 with a mean below 10−3, and 31.3% [23.3, 40.3] on the 556 with neither.

objections.objection: While the text acknowledges that a per-cell failure does not invalidate the aggregate rank tests, the abstract's phrasing could easily be misinterpreted by a casual reader as invalidating the papers' core claims.
objections.what_would_fix_it: Add a brief clause to the abstract explicitly stating that because metaheuristics claims are typically aggregate (e.g., Friedman over 30 functions), a per-cell Welch failure does not necessarily refute the paper's primary algorithmic claim.
objections.quote: a per-cell check of printed evidence, not of aggregate rank tests.

questions_to_authors: Is the audit fair? Yes and no. It is fair to audit what authors actually print on the page. However, auditing heavy-tailed CEC benchmark data using a Welch's t-test—a test our community explicitly abandoned 15 years ago for this exact reason—feels like a category error, even if you acknowledge it is 'the only test the printed summaries admit.' Does a per-cell Welch test of a bold mean say anything about the paper's aggregate claim? As you rightly note in the discussion, no. My algorithms are validated by a Friedman rank over 30 or 50 functions; a Welch failure on F14 does not invalidate the paper. Would the recommendations change what you do? Yes, your recommendation to enforce the +/-/= notation per cell (or release per-run values) is excellent and reinforces the Derrac/García guidelines. What would make you dismiss the paper? I would dismiss this paper if it is published without human validation of the LLM table reader. You cannot publish a 'gotcha' audit of the literature where the load-bearing data extraction is performed by an unverified generative AI.
